title: HANNAH WAS LOVED BY HER HUSBAND… SO WHY DID GOD ALLOW ANOTHER WOMAN TO BREAK HER HEART?
paragraphs: HANNAH WAS LOVED BY HER HUSBAND… SO WHY DID GOD ALLOW ANOTHER WOMAN TO BREAK HER HEART?

The painful marriage story behind 1 Samuel 1 reveals what happens when love cannot heal your deepest wound, your rival knows exactly where to hurt you, and heaven seems silent while your tears keep falling.
Imagine being loved by someone who cannot understand why you are still crying.
Imagine sitting at a family table where everyone else seems to have what you have spent years begging God to give you.
Imagine watching another woman enjoy the very blessing you desperately desire.
Now imagine that woman knows your pain.
And instead of showing compassion, she uses it against you.
Not once.
Not accidentally.
Year after year.
And the hardest part?
The man who loves you sees your tears, tries to comfort you, and still cannot understand the depth of what is happening inside your heart.
That was Hannah's world.
Before she became the mother of Samuel, one of Israel's great prophets, she was a wounded woman living inside a complicated marriage.
Before her prayer became famous, her pain was familiar.
Before Scripture recorded her song of victory, it recorded her tears.
And hidden inside this ancient household is a truth that may confront everything you believe about unanswered prayer, marriage, jealousy, suffering, and the silence of God.
Because Hannah's story is not simply about a woman who wanted a baby.
It is about a woman who was loved but still hurting.
A woman who worshiped while wounded.
A woman whose rival could reach places her husband could not heal.
And a God who heard a prayer that no human being could even hear.
But to understand why Hannah suffered so deeply, we must first enter the marriage that made her suffering so complicated.
There were two women in one household. One had children. The other had her husband's special affection. Neither possessed everything she wanted.
First Samuel 1:2 introduces a man named Elkanah:
"He had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children." (1 Samuel 1:2, KJV)
Read that carefully.
The Bible introduces the women through a painful contrast.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah had none.
Later, Scripture reveals that Elkanah loved Hannah and gave her a special portion of the sacrificial meal.
The household contained two forms of blessing, but neither blessing guaranteed peace.
One woman possessed the motherhood Hannah longed for.
The other possessed a special place in Elkanah's affections.
And somewhere between those unequal circumstances, a rivalry grew.
We must be careful here. Scripture never explicitly says Peninnah was jealous of Elkanah's love for Hannah. It also does not tell us which woman Elkanah married first or why he married two women.
Those details are often supplied by preachers, dramatizations, and imagined backstories.
But they are not stated in 1 Samuel 1.
What Scripture does reveal is already heartbreaking enough.
Elkanah's polygamous household became the setting for deep relational suffering.
Polygamy existed in ancient Israel, and the Old Testament records its presence without portraying every recorded practice as God's ideal.
Jesus later directed attention back to God's creation design for marriage, where a man and woman become one flesh (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6).
The Bible does not ask us to romanticize the brokenness inside Elkanah's home.
It invites us to see what happened there.
Because a family can be religious and still be wounded.
A husband can be affectionate and still be unable to meet every emotional need.
A household can participate in worship while carrying years of unresolved cruelty.
And someone can sit beside you in a sacred place while silently fighting a battle you cannot see.
Peninnah had what Hannah wanted. But instead of becoming a source of compassion, she became a source of torment.
First Samuel 1:6 says:
"And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb." (KJV)
The Hebrew language makes the hostility especially striking.
The word translated "adversary" is צָרָתָהּ (tsaratah), referring to her rival or female adversary.
The verse also uses the Hebrew expression כַּעַס (ka'as), associated with vexation, irritation, and distress.
The text describes deliberate provocation.
Peninnah was not merely celebrating her own children.
She was intentionally distressing Hannah over her childlessness.
Think about the cruelty of that.
Hannah did not need anyone to remind her that she had no children.
She knew.
She knew when she woke up.
She knew when she saw other mothers.
She knew when another year passed.
She knew when she returned to worship carrying the same unanswered longing.
And Peninnah knew too.
Sometimes the deepest wounds are inflicted by people who know exactly where we are vulnerable.
Not every painful word comes from an enemy.
Sometimes it comes from someone sharing your home, your family gatherings, or your place of worship.
Someone who knows your history.
Someone who knows what you have been praying about.
Someone who knows what makes your voice tremble.
And instead of protecting that vulnerable place, they press against it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You have been asked why you are still single.
Why you have not had a child.
Why your marriage has not improved.
Why you are still struggling financially.
Why you have not recovered.
Why you are not as successful as someone else.
And the question sounds innocent to everyone listening.
But you know what it does to you.
You know the nights you have cried about it.
You know how many times you have already brought it before God.
You know how much strength it takes not to break down in front of everyone.
Hannah knew that pain.
But here is something important.
Peninnah's cruelty was her own moral responsibility. Hannah's suffering was not evidence that she deserved it.
Scripture says the Lord had closed Hannah's womb. That is part of the biblical narrative, and we should not erase it.
But the passage does not tell us why God permitted Hannah's childlessness for those years.
It does not say Hannah had committed some secret sin.
It does not say she lacked faith.
It does not say her suffering was punishment.
And it certainly does not say Peninnah was authorized to torment her.
The Bible distinguishes God's sovereignty from human cruelty.
God's authority over Hannah's circumstances did not make Peninnah's behavior righteous.
That distinction matters.
Because some wounded believers have been taught to interpret every painful circumstance as evidence that God is angry with them.
But Hannah's story does not support that conclusion.
Neither does the Gospel.
When Jesus encountered a man born blind, He rejected the assumption that the man's condition must have resulted from his own sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1–3).
Suffering is not a reliable measurement of someone's spiritual standing.
And infertility is never a measure of a woman's worth.
Hannah was not less valuable because she had no child.
Her dignity did not begin when Samuel was born.
She was already a person worthy of compassion before her circumstances changed.
Please hear that.
You do not have to receive the blessing you are waiting for before your life becomes precious to God.
Now consider the timing of Peninnah's provocation.
First Samuel 1:7 says this continued year after year, especially as the family went up to the house of the Lord.
The place where Hannah came to worship was also a place where her grief intensified.
Imagine preparing for a sacred journey.
Perhaps hoping this year would be different.
Perhaps telling yourself you would remain strong.
Perhaps believing you could get through the gathering without crying.
Then the familiar hostility begins.
A remark.
A comparison.
A reminder.
And suddenly the pain you tried to contain rises to the surface.
Scripture tells us Hannah wept and would not eat.
Her suffering affected her appetite.
It affected her participation in a family celebration.
It affected the way she experienced what should have been a joyful occasion.
This was not a passing disappointment.
It was persistent grief.
And then Elkanah spoke.
His words are among the most revealing sentences in the entire story.
"Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?" (1 Samuel 1:8, KJV)
There is tenderness in his concern.
He notices her tears.
He wants her to eat.
He wants her to recognize his love.
But there is also a painful limitation in his question.
Elkanah seems to believe that his affection should be enough to comfort her.
He cannot fully understand why the love he offers does not remove the grief she carries.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Have you ever been loved and still felt lonely?
Have you ever had people tell you how blessed you were while you were silently grieving something they could not replace?
Have you ever heard someone say, "But you have so much to be thankful for," when you were trying to explain the one thing that kept breaking your heart?
Gratitude and grief can exist together.
Love and longing can exist together.
Faith and tears can exist together.
Hannah could appreciate her husband without pretending her desire for a child had disappeared.
And Elkanah's love, however genuine, could not solve everything.
There are wounds a spouse cannot heal.
There are burdens a friend cannot remove.
There are questions no human reassurance can fully answer.
That does not make human love worthless.
It simply reminds us that human love is limited.
Only God can occupy the place that belongs to God.
But even that truth must be handled carefully.
We should never use spiritual language to dismiss another person's pain.
Telling someone to trust God is not a substitute for listening.
Quoting Scripture is not permission to ignore cruelty.
And encouraging prayer does not excuse a family from its responsibility to protect someone who is being mistreated.
Elkanah's household needed more than religious activity.
It needed compassion and righteousness.
Then Hannah did something that changed the direction of her story.
She got up.
First Samuel 1:9 records that after the meal at Shiloh, Hannah rose.
It is a small movement in the narrative.
But it leads to one of the most moving prayers in Scripture.
She went before the Lord.
Not because the problem had been resolved.
Not because Peninnah had apologized.
Not because Elkanah finally understood everything.
Not because she had received a promise that she would conceive.
She went while she was still hurting.
First Samuel 1:10 says:
"And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is מָרַת נָפֶשׁ (marat nefesh), describing a person deeply embittered or distressed in soul.
It does not mean Hannah was necessarily bitter against God.
It describes the anguish of her condition.
This was not a polished prayer.
It was not a performance.
It was not a carefully rehearsed speech designed to impress religious people.
It was the cry of a wounded woman.
And something extraordinary happened.
Her lips moved.
But her voice was not heard.
Eli, the priest, watched her and wrongly assumed she was drunk.
Think about that.
Hannah had been misunderstood at home.
Now she was misunderstood at the sanctuary.
The woman who came to pour out her heart before God was accused of behaving shamefully.
Even in a sacred place, someone misread her suffering.
Perhaps you have experienced something similar.
You finally gathered enough courage to speak.
And someone judged your tears.
You tried to explain your exhaustion.
And someone called you dramatic.
You admitted that you were struggling.
And someone questioned your faith.
Hannah could have withdrawn.
She could have allowed Eli's accusation to silence her.
Instead, she answered with dignity.
"No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD." (1 Samuel 1:15, KJV)
"I have poured out my soul before the LORD."
The Hebrew wording includes וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי (va'eshpokh et-nafshi).
The verb conveys pouring out.
Her nefesh—her soul, her very self—was being poured before God.
What an image.
Not hiding the pain.
Not disguising the disappointment.
Not pretending everything was fine.
Pouring it out.
Some of us have become experts at appearing strong.
We know how to smile at church.
We know how to answer, "I'm blessed."
We know how to encourage everyone else.
We know how to post Bible verses while carrying private grief.
But there comes a moment when the soul grows tired of pretending.
Hannah teaches us that reverence does not require emotional dishonesty.
You can approach God with trembling faith.
You can pray while crying.
You can worship without understanding.
You can bring Him questions you do not know how to answer.
The Psalms repeatedly demonstrate that faithful prayer can include lament, confusion, sorrow, and desperate appeals for help.
God does not require you to manufacture happiness before coming to Him.
He calls you to come truthfully.
And here is the detail that should stop us.
Hannah's circumstances had not yet changed when her countenance changed.
After Eli spoke a blessing over her, Scripture says:
"So the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad." (1 Samuel 1:18, KJV)
She had not yet conceived.
She had not yet held Samuel.
She had not yet watched Peninnah's provocation lose its power.
She had prayed.
She had received a word of blessing.
And she went away able to eat again.
We should not pretend this means every believer will immediately feel better after praying.
The Bible does not promise that every episode of grief will disappear in one moment.
But Hannah's experience shows something beautiful.
Her circumstances remained unresolved, yet she was no longer carrying her sorrow in exactly the same way.
Prayer had become the place where her anguish was brought into God's presence.
Sometimes God's people experience peace before they receive an answer.
Sometimes they must continue trusting while the pain remains.
And sometimes the faithful thing is to seek help, receive comfort, and keep walking one day at a time.
None of those experiences makes a believer less loved.
Now we must confront one of the most difficult questions in Hannah's story.
Why did God allow the suffering to continue for so long?
The text does not give us a complete explanation.
And we must resist the temptation to invent one.
It would be easy to declare that God allowed Peninnah to torment Hannah specifically to make her pray harder.
But Scripture never says that.
It would be easy to claim that every painful rival is secretly assigned by God to push someone toward destiny.
But the Bible does not teach that as a universal principle.
It would also be dangerous to suggest that abuse or cruelty should simply be endured because God might use it.
God can work redemptively through suffering without approving the evil that causes it.
What we can say is that the Lord heard Hannah.
First Samuel 1:19 records that the Lord remembered her.
In biblical language, divine remembrance does not imply that God had forgotten her existence.
It expresses His purposeful attention and action.
The Hebrew verb זָכַר (zakhar) means to remember, and in this context it introduces God's gracious response to Hannah.
The narrative continues:

"Wherefore it came to pass, when the time was come about after Hannah had conceived, that she bare a son, and called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked him of the LORD." (1 Samuel 1:20, KJV)
Hannah received the child for whom she had prayed.
But notice what Scripture does not teach.
It does not teach that every woman who prays like Hannah will conceive.
It does not teach that childlessness is always temporary.
It does not teach that enough tears, faith, or vows can compel God to grant a specific request.
Hannah's experience is a true account of God's action in her life, not a formula that guarantees identical outcomes for everyone.
And that matters profoundly for those who have prayed for years and are still waiting.
For the woman who has endured another disappointing medical appointment.
For the couple who has quietly grieved pregnancy loss.
For the person whose marriage did not survive.
For the believer who prayed for healing and still lives with illness.
For the parent whose child has not returned home.
For the person who prayed for a loved one who nevertheless died.
Hannah's story should never become another Peninnah-like weapon against someone who is suffering.
We must not use her answered prayer to shame those whose prayers remain unanswered.
The Christian hope is greater than the promise of receiving every earthly blessing we desire.
It is the promise that God has acted decisively for our salvation through Jesus Christ and will ultimately make all things new.
And this is where Hannah's story opens into something much larger than one household.
Hannah's son Samuel would become a prophet and judge in Israel.
He would later anoint David as king.
And from David's royal line, according to the Scriptures, the Messiah would come.
Hannah could not have seen the full historical significance of the child she held.
She knew she had prayed.
She knew God had answered.
She knew the boy belonged ultimately to the Lord.
And she honored her vow by bringing Samuel to serve at the sanctuary under Eli's care.
Her prayer had begun with a request for a son.
Her response to God's answer became an act of dedication.
Then, in 1 Samuel 2, Hannah sang.
The woman introduced through weeping became a woman whose words proclaimed the holiness, sovereignty, and saving power of God.
Her song declares:
"There is none holy as the LORD: for there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God." (1 Samuel 2:2, KJV)
And later:
"He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory." (1 Samuel 2:8, KJV)
Her song celebrates the God who overturns human pride and lifts the lowly.
Centuries later, Mary's song in Luke 1 would echo strikingly similar themes.
Mary rejoiced in the God who regards the humble and reverses human expectations.
Through Mary, Jesus Christ entered the world.
And in Jesus, we encounter the deepest fulfillment of the hope that runs through Scripture.
Not merely that God can reverse earthly circumstances.
But that God has come to rescue sinners.
That grace reaches people who cannot save themselves.
That the proud are called to repentance.
That the broken are invited to come.
That forgiveness is available through the crucified and risen Savior.
And that death itself will not have the final word.
Hannah's story is not a direct prophecy that every wounded person will receive a Samuel.
But it belongs to the biblical story that ultimately leads us to Christ.
And there is another connection we dare not miss.
Hannah was misunderstood by a priest who thought her distress was drunkenness.
Jesus, our great High Priest, is not ignorant of human weakness.
Hebrews 4:15–16 teaches that Christ can sympathize with our weaknesses and invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence.
Hannah came to the sanctuary with a burden that human beings struggled to understand.
Through Christ, believers have access to the Father, whose mercy does not depend on our ability to explain our pain perfectly.
And Jesus knows suffering from the inside.
He was rejected.
He was falsely accused.
He was mocked.
He was betrayed.
He wept.
He endured the cross.
Not because He was powerless, but because He willingly gave Himself to accomplish our redemption.
The cross tells us something Hannah's story alone cannot fully reveal.
God's love is not measured by how quickly He removes our suffering. It is revealed supremely in the Savior who gave Himself for us.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Before you were healed.
Before you understood.
Before your life became orderly.
Before you knew how to pray properly.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that Jesus exists to fulfill every desire we bring to Him.
But that through His death and resurrection, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life to all who repent and believe.
This is why our theme is more than a memorable phrase.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending our wounds never happened.
He redeems sinners.
He restores our relationship with God.
He transforms lives through His Spirit.
And He promises a future in which sorrow and death will finally be defeated.
Hannah's marriage story also contains a warning we must not overlook.
Do not become Peninnah in someone else's story.
Do not turn another person's unanswered prayer into a comparison.
Do not use your marriage to shame someone who is single.
Do not use your children to diminish someone struggling with infertility.
Do not use your financial success to humiliate someone who is poor.
Do not use your ministry, knowledge, or spiritual experiences to make another believer feel worthless.
And do not assume that because God has blessed you in one area, you are spiritually superior to someone who has not received the same blessing.
Peninnah had children.
That was a blessing.
But possessing a blessing did not justify her cruelty.
A gift from God should never become a weapon against another human being.
And if you recognize yourself in Peninnah's behavior, the answer is not to hide behind excuses.
Repent.
Confess the wrong.
Stop the cruelty.
Where appropriate and safe, seek to make things right with those you have hurt.
The Gospel does not merely comfort victims of sin.
It also calls those who commit sin to turn from it.
Perhaps you identify more with Elkanah.
You genuinely love someone.
You want to help.
You cannot understand why your affection has not fixed their sadness.
Then learn from his limitations.
Sometimes the most loving response is not another explanation.
It is listening.
It is refusing to minimize grief.
It is taking mistreatment seriously.
It is acknowledging that someone's pain may be real even when you cannot personally experience it.
And perhaps you are Hannah.
You are tired.
You have been faithful in ways nobody notices.
You have prayed prayers nobody has heard.
You have watched other people celebrate blessings you are still waiting for.
You have tried to rejoice with those who rejoice, even when their joy reminds you of your own grief.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you feel guilty for hurting.
You think a stronger Christian would not cry so much.
You think a more faithful believer would have stopped asking questions.
You think your sadness means you have disappointed God.
But remember Hannah.
She wept.
She could not eat.
She prayed out of anguish.
And Scripture did not erase her tears to make her faith look impressive.
Her tears are part of the testimony.
Your tears are not proof that you have abandoned God.
The question is what you will do with your pain.
Will you allow it to become bitterness toward others?
Will you let comparison determine your worth?
Will you begin believing that God owes you the exact life someone else has received?
Or will you bring your wounded heart honestly before the Lord?
Not with a demand that He follow your timetable.
Not with a bargain that tries to purchase His favor.
But with faith that says:
"Lord, You know what I desire. You know what I have endured. You know what I cannot explain. Teach me to trust You, even when I do not understand."
That is not a weak prayer.
It is a deeply human prayer of surrender.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not mistake Christianity for a promise that your circumstances will immediately improve.
Jesus calls us to something greater and more costly.
Repent of sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Him.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And learn to live under His lordship, whether the season brings abundance or loss.
Because the greatest miracle in Hannah's story was not that human worth could finally be established through childbirth.
Her worth was never dependent on childbirth.
The extraordinary gift was that God acted graciously in her circumstances and incorporated her family into His unfolding purposes for Israel.
And the greater miracle offered through Christ is that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
That is the grace worth proclaiming.
That is the truth worth carrying into a wounded world.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with emotional religious content that disappears when they close their phones.
But to keep directing hearts back to Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, biblical discipleship, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who look completely fine.
But privately, they are Hannah.
Their marriages are struggling.
Their prayers seem unanswered.
Their families do not understand them.
Their faith is exhausted.
And sometimes one biblically faithful message reaches them at the moment they are ready to give up.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because truth shared with love can reach someone who might never walk into a church or ask openly for prayer.
You do not have to share private details.

And if God has carried you through a season of grief, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading silently may need to know that faithful people can struggle, weep, seek help, and still find strength in the Lord.
And if these messages have helped you grow in faith, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
It can help keep Scripture-centered encouragement reaching people who need it.
It can support the development of teaching materials.
It can help make discipleship resources more accessible.
And it can allow you to participate in a shared effort to proclaim Christ faithfully.
Those free resources remain an important part of our mission.
These products are simply resources and reminders. They are not measures of spiritual maturity, and purchasing them is never a condition of receiving God's grace.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share the truth matters.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
And the purpose of every faithful Christian ministry should be to point people toward Him, not make people dependent on the ministry itself.
Now, before you leave, return with me to Hannah.
Picture her one more time.
Not holding Samuel.
Not singing her song.
Not standing in the moment of answered prayer.
Picture her earlier.
In the sanctuary.
Her lips moving.
Her eyes wet.
Her heart aching.
A priest misunderstanding her.
A rival tormenting her.
A husband unable to remove her grief.
And no child yet in her arms.
She did not know what the next chapter would contain.
She did not know how her story would be remembered.
She did not know that generations of wounded believers would someday read about her tears and find courage to pray.
All she knew was that she needed God.
And she came.
That may be the most important part of her story for you today.
Not the moment she received what she wanted.
But the moment she brought her broken heart before the Lord without knowing what He would do next.
Because some of you are still living in that moment.
You have not received the answer.
The relationship has not been restored.
The diagnosis has not changed.
The grief has not disappeared.
The person who hurt you has not apologized.
And you are wondering whether God still sees you.
The Gospel does not authorize me to promise that tomorrow everything will change.
But it gives me every reason to point you toward Jesus Christ.
The Savior who knows suffering.
The Lord who welcomes the weary.
The Redeemer who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness.
The risen King who will one day make all things new.
So come to Him.
Not because your tears guarantee a particular outcome.
But because He is worthy of your trust even when the outcome is unknown.
Come with your questions.
Come with your repentance.
Come with your exhaustion.
Come with your longing.
Come with the parts of your story you are afraid to say aloud.
And remember this:
Hannah's unanswered years did not mean she was unseen, and your unfinished story does not mean Christ has abandoned you.
